The income a business earns from its ordinary activities — selling goods, providing services, earning fees or interest — measured at the amount it expects to be entitled to, after deducting returns, discounts and rebates.
The value of goods or services sold to customers in a period.
In British and Commonwealth usage, the total revenue of a business in a period.
Revenue minus cost of goods sold (or cost of sales).

terms.def: Profit from the company’s core operations after deducting cost of sales and all operating expenses, including depreciation and amortisation, but before interest and tax.

terms.def: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation.

terms.cat: Profit layers: gross profit to net income

terms.cat: Profit layers: gross profit to net income

terms.cat: Cash flow, working capital, CAPEX and OPEX

terms.def: Ongoing costs of running the business that are expensed in the period they are incurred: salaries, rent, utilities, marketing, software subscriptions, maintenance, travel.

terms.cat: Receivables, payables, liquidity, solvency and leverage

terms.cat: Receivables, payables, liquidity, solvency and leverage

terms.def: The use of borrowed money (financial leverage) or fixed costs (operating leverage) to magnify returns.
terms.cat: Receivables, payables, liquidity, solvency and leverage

terms.def: A profit measure expressed as a percentage of revenue (selling price).
The amount added to cost to arrive at a selling price, expressed as a percentage of cost.
The gain (or loss) from an investment relative to its cost: ROI = (gain from investment − cost of investment) ÷ cost of investment.
Net income divided by average shareholders’ equity.
The logic by which an organisation creates value for customers, delivers it, and captures part of that value as revenue and profit.
The specific benefit a product or service promises a defined customer, and why that customer should choose it over alternatives.
Any person or group that affects or is affected by an organisation’s decisions: shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, lenders, regulators, communities.
The 12-month period a company uses for accounting and reporting.
The period from the start of the current financial year to a given date, used to report cumulative results.
An annualised figure extrapolated from recent results, e.g., this month’s revenue × 12.
The reduction in average cost per unit as output increases, because fixed costs are spread over more units and larger buyers obtain better terms.
A company’s sales as a percentage of total sales in a defined market.
Ongoing business costs not directly tied to producing a specific product or service: rent, administration, management salaries, insurance, utilities.
A standard or point of reference against which performance, prices or practices are compared.
A structured investigation of a company, asset, counterparty or transaction before committing, to verify facts and uncover risks.
A document recording the intentions and main terms agreed between parties, usually expressed to be non-binding except for specific clauses (confidentiality, exclusivity, governing law).
An owner of shares (equity) in a company, entitled to rights defined by law and the company’s constitution: voting, dividends, and a residual claim on assets after creditors.
The body elected by shareholders to oversee management, set strategy, approve major decisions and protect the company’s interests.
The most senior executive responsible for running the company and implementing the board’s strategy.
The principle that shareholders’ losses are limited to the amount they invested in the company;
A company whose main purpose is to own shares in other companies (subsidiaries) and often to control them.
A legal entity created for a single, limited purpose — to hold an asset, ring-fence a project, or carry out a financing — isolating its risks from the sponsor.
The system of rules, practices and processes by which a company is directed and controlled, balancing the interests of shareholders, management and other stakeholders.

The company’s constitutional document setting rules for share classes, shareholder meetings, board powers, transfers of shares and other internal matters (names vary: bylaws, memorandum and articles, statutes).
A distribution of a company’s profits to its shareholders, usually in cash and in proportion to shareholdings.
The amount contributed by shareholders in exchange for shares, recorded in equity.
Recording revenues when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash is received or paid.
The system in which every transaction is recorded in at least two accounts, with total debits equal to total credits, keeping Assets = Liabilities + Equity in balance.

A resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events, from which future economic benefits are expected (IFRS Conceptual Framework: a present economic resource with the potential to produce economic benefits).
A present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events: loans, payables, taxes owed, provisions, deferred revenue.
The residual interest in the assets after deducting liabilities: share capital, retained earnings and other reserves.
The systematic allocation of the cost of a tangible fixed asset, less residual value, over its useful life.
(1) The systematic allocation of the cost of an intangible asset with a finite life (software, licences, patents).
A reduction in the carrying amount of an asset to its recoverable amount when that amount is lower than the book value.

A liability of uncertain timing or amount (IAS 37), recognised when there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow is probable and the amount can be reliably estimated — e.g., warranties, legal claims, restructuring.
Cash received (or receivable) for goods or services not yet delivered;
The direct costs of the goods sold in a period: purchase or production cost, inbound freight, duties and other costs to bring inventory to its present location and condition.
Cumulative net income kept in the company after dividends since inception;
The excess of the price paid in a business combination over the fair value of identifiable net assets acquired;
The independent auditor’s conclusion on whether financial statements are presented fairly, in all material respects, under the applicable framework.
The principle that a sum of money today is worth more than the same sum in the future, because it can be invested to earn a return and because of inflation and risk.
The sum of the present values of all expected cash flows of a project or investment, including the initial outlay, discounted at an appropriate rate.
The discount rate at which a project’s NPV equals zero — the annualised return implied by its cash flows.
The average rate of return a company must pay its capital providers, weighted by the market values of debt and equity, with the cost of debt taken after tax.
Cash generated after operating expenses, taxes, working-capital investment and capital expenditure — the cash available to repay debt, pay dividends or invest.
The value of a company’s operating business to all capital providers: equity value + net debt (+ minority interests + preferred equity, − non-operating assets as appropriate).
Total interest-bearing debt minus cash and cash equivalents.
The minimum acceptable rate of return for an investment, set by the company or investor, often WACC plus a risk premium.
The time required for cumulative cash inflows from a project to recover the initial investment.
The mix of debt and equity (and hybrid instruments) used to finance a company’s assets.
A group of investments with similar characteristics and behaviour: equities, fixed income, cash, real estate, commodities, private equity, hedge funds, infrastructure.
Spreading investments across assets whose returns are not perfectly correlated to reduce portfolio risk without proportionally reducing expected return.
The degree of variation of an asset’s price or return over time, usually measured as the annualised standard deviation of returns.
The income return on an investment, expressed as a percentage of its price or value: dividend yield, current yield, yield to maturity on bonds.
One hundredth of one percentage point (0.01%).
Share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding: the market value of a listed company’s equity.
The ability to buy or sell an asset quickly in size without moving its price significantly;
Taking a position that offsets an existing exposure to reduce risk from price, currency, interest-rate or commodity movements.
An arrangement under which a bank makes credit available to a borrower up to an agreed limit, on agreed terms — e.g., overdraft, revolving credit, term loan, trade-finance lines, guarantee lines.

terms.ar: الحساب الجاري المدين / السحب على المكشوف
terms.def: A facility allowing a current account to go into a negative balance up to an agreed limit;

A committed facility under which a borrower can draw, repay and redraw loans up to a limit during an availability period (often 1–5 years), paying interest on drawn amounts and a commitment fee on undrawn amounts.
A loan of a fixed amount for a fixed period, repaid by instalments (amortising) or at maturity (bullet), typically used to finance capex, acquisitions or long-term needs.
The length of time until a loan, bill, letter of credit or other credit instrument matures.

Assets pledged by a borrower to secure an obligation, which the lender can enforce against if the borrower defaults: property mortgages, pledges of shares, cash deposits, assignments of receivables, charges over inventory or equipment.

An irrevocable undertaking by a bank to pay a beneficiary up to a stated amount if the applicant fails to perform an obligation, typically payable on first written demand (demand guarantee, often subject to URDG 758).
A promise in a loan agreement by the borrower to do (positive covenant), not to do (negative covenant), or to maintain financial ratios (financial covenant).
Floating-rate loans are priced as a reference (benchmark) rate plus a credit margin.
A bank’s undertaking, on behalf of the buyer (applicant), to pay the seller (beneficiary) a stated sum against presentation of complying documents within a set time, usually subject to UCP 600.
A bank that provides services (payments, account holding, trade finance) on behalf of another bank, usually in another country or currency.

Procedures by which financial institutions verify the identity of clients, understand ownership and control, the nature of the business and the expected activity, and assess money-laundering and sanctions risk.
A loan provided by a group (syndicate) of lenders under one agreement, arranged by one or more lead arrangers and administered by an agent bank.
A loan on which the borrower is in default or unlikely to pay, commonly defined as 90 or more days past due or classified as credit-impaired (Stage 3 under IFRS 9).
The rate at which the general level of prices for goods and services rises, reducing the purchasing power of money.
Nominal values are measured in current money;
The total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a period.
Actions by a central bank to influence money supply, interest rates and credit conditions to achieve price stability and other mandates.
Government decisions on spending, taxation and borrowing to influence the economy.
The price of one currency in terms of another.
The percentage change in quantity demanded resulting from a 1% change in price (price elasticity) or another variable (income, prices of substitutes).
A significant, broad-based decline in economic activity lasting more than a few months;
The record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world: current account (trade, income, transfers), capital account and financial account.
The organisation of a market by the number and size of firms, product differentiation and entry barriers: perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, monopoly.
Total sales and marketing cost incurred to acquire new customers in a period divided by the number of new customers acquired.
The present value of the gross profit (or contribution) a customer is expected to generate over the whole relationship.
The stages a prospect passes through from first awareness to purchase, with conversion rates between stages (e.g., lead → qualified lead → opportunity → proposal → won).
A person or organisation that has shown potential interest in buying, or that matches the target profile, but has not yet been qualified.
Dividing a market into groups of customers with similar needs, behaviours or characteristics, so products, prices and messages can be tailored.
The rate at which customers stop buying or cancel subscriptions in a period (customer churn), or the share of recurring revenue lost (revenue churn).
A strategic approach to managing a company’s most important customers with dedicated teams, plans and senior relationships.
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement: what you will do if this negotiation fails.
Zone of possible agreement: the range between the seller’s minimum acceptable price and the buyer’s maximum, within which a deal can be made.
A seller’s statement of the price and terms on which it is willing to supply specified goods or services, usually with a validity period.
The agreed conditions for when and how payment is made: timing (advance, at sight, net 30/60/90), method (transfer, L/C, collection), currency, and discounts or penalties.
The time between initiating a process (placing an order) and its completion (receipt of goods).
Extra inventory held to protect against variability in demand and lead time.
The inventory level at which a new order should be placed: expected demand during lead time plus safety stock.

The total cost of a product delivered to the buyer’s premises: purchase price + freight + insurance + duties and taxes (non-recoverable) + port, clearance and handling charges + inland transport + financing and other costs.
COGS divided by average inventory: how many times inventory is sold and replaced in a period.
Outsourced logistics services — warehousing, transport, fulfilment, customs — provided by a specialised company.

Eleven ICC rules defining the obligations, costs and risk transfer between seller and buyer for delivery of goods: EXW, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU, DDP (any mode) and FAS, FOB, CFR, CIF (sea and inland waterway).

A document issued by a carrier (or its agent) for sea transport that serves as (1) receipt for goods shipped, (2) evidence of the contract of carriage, and (3) when negotiable (“to order”), a document of title that controls the goods.
The value of imported goods for calculating ad valorem duty, primarily the transaction value (price actually paid or payable) with adjustments, under the WTO Customs Valuation Agreement.

The Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System maintained by the World Customs Organization: a 6-digit international product classification, extended to 8–12 digits nationally, used to determine tariffs, controls and statistics.
A company that arranges the transport of goods on behalf of shippers: booking carriers, consolidating cargo, preparing documents, arranging insurance, customs clearance and delivery.
Charges for using carrier-owned containers beyond agreed free time: demurrage typically applies while a full container remains in the port/terminal;
Statements of fact made by a party in a contract (representations) and contractual promises that certain facts are true (warranties).
A contractual promise by one party to compensate the other for specified losses, often on a pound-for-pound basis, regardless of whether a breach occurred.
A contract clause excusing or suspending performance when events beyond a party’s reasonable control (war, natural disaster, epidemic, government action) prevent performance.
A clause capping the amount and/or types of loss a party can be liable for (e.g., cap at contract value;
Conditions that must be satisfied (or waived) before an obligation becomes effective — e.g., regulatory approval, board approval, delivery of security documents before a loan can be drawn.
Governing law is the legal system that interprets the contract;
A private dispute-resolution process in which parties agree to submit disputes to one or more arbitrators whose award is binding and generally enforceable internationally.

Provisions setting out when and how a party may end a contract — for convenience, for material breach (often after a cure period), insolvency, change of control or prolonged force majeure — and the consequences.
The risk that the other party to a contract or transaction fails to perform: does not pay, deliver, or honour a derivative or guarantee.
The risk of loss because a borrower or customer fails to meet payment obligations.
The risk of loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems, or from external events (Basel definition, which includes legal risk but excludes strategic and reputational risk).
Ensuring that an organisation follows applicable laws, regulations, standards and internal policies, and managing the risk of non-compliance.
Laws, regulations and procedures to prevent criminals from disguising illegally obtained funds as legitimate income.

Restrictive measures imposed by governments or international bodies (e.g., the UN Security Council, the US through OFAC, the EU, the UK) against countries, entities, individuals, vessels or sectors: asset freezes, trade bans, financial restrictions.
A document listing identified risks with their causes, likelihood, impact, rating, owner, controls and actions.
The price paid by the insured to the insurer for coverage over a period.
The portion of each loss borne by the insured before the insurer pays (called “excess” in UK usage).
A provision in an insurance policy that removes specified perils, property or circumstances from coverage.
The process by which an insurer (or a bank, for securities and loans) assesses a risk, decides whether to accept it, and sets terms and price.
Insurance purchased by insurers to transfer part of their risk to reinsurers.
The insurer’s right, after paying a claim, to step into the insured’s position and recover the loss from a responsible third party.
A quantifiable measure used to evaluate progress toward an important objective.
A goal-setting framework pairing a qualitative objective with 2–5 measurable key results, usually set quarterly.
The formal framework specifying which roles may approve which decisions and commitments, up to which limits.
Identifying stakeholders, understanding their interests and influence, and planning engagement to secure support and manage resistance.
A matrix assigning, for each task or decision, who is Responsible (does it), Accountable (owns the outcome — one person), Consulted and Informed.
An attribute that allows a company to earn higher returns than competitors over time — typically through lower cost, differentiation, or focus on a niche.
A durable structural advantage that protects a company’s profits from competitors: network effects, switching costs, intangible assets (brands, patents, licences), cost advantages, efficient scale.

terms.ar: تحليل نقاط القوة والضعف والفرص والتهديدات
terms.def: A framework listing internal Strengths and Weaknesses and external Opportunities and Threats.

A framework for analysing industry attractiveness through five forces: rivalry among competitors, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers.
A scan of external macro-environment factors: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental.

terms.ar: الحد الأدنى من المنتج القابل للتطبيق
terms.def: The simplest version of a product that allows a team to test a key hypothesis with real users and learn with the least effort.
The state in which a product satisfies a strong market demand, shown by retention, organic growth, willingness to pay and customer pull.
Burn rate is the net cash a company spends per month;

A document summarising the key terms of a proposed investment or financing (valuation, amount, instrument, rights, conditions), mostly non-binding except for clauses like confidentiality and exclusivity.
Pre-money valuation is the company’s value before new investment;
An integrated software system that manages core business processes — finance, procurement, inventory, sales, manufacturing, HR — on a shared database.
A defined interface allowing software systems to request data or services from each other.
Software delivered over the internet on a subscription basis and hosted by the provider.
Protection of systems, networks and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access.
Methods that let computers learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed with rules.
Technology-enabled financial services and the companies that provide them: digital payments, lending platforms, neobanks, wealth tech, insurtech, regtech.
Technologies and practices for collecting, integrating, analysing and presenting business data to support decisions — dashboards, reports, ad hoc analysis.
Descriptive analytics explains what happened;
Tracking groups of customers who share a starting characteristic (e.g., month of acquisition) over time to measure retention, revenue and behaviour.
Buying, transporting, storing, blending and selling actual commodities (as opposed to only trading financial contracts), earning margins from location, time, quality and logistics arbitrage.
A published reference price for a commodity used to price physical contracts and derivatives — e.g., Brent and WTI for crude oil, LME prices for base metals, exchange futures for grains.
The difference between the local physical (cash) price of a commodity and the price of a related futures contract: basis = cash − futures.
Contango: futures prices for later delivery are higher than nearer ones (upward-sloping forward curve).
Laytime is the time allowed in a charter party for loading and discharging;
Net income; also “the final result” of any discussion.
Revenue.
Number of employees (sometimes FTEs).
Workload expressed as full-time positions (two half-time staff = 1 FTE).
A defined output promised in a project or contract.
Final date for delivery.
Time between order and delivery.
Rough estimate.
Quick rough calculation.
Practical heuristic, not exact.
Sequence of activities that create value (Porter).

terms.ar: من شركة إلى شركة / إلى مستهلك / إلى حكومة
terms.def: Customer type in the business model.
Assumption the business will continue operating for the foreseeable future.
Main activity generating most value.
Asset not essential to the core business; often a divestment candidate.
Contracting an external provider to perform a function.
Moving activities to another country.
Ability to grow volume without proportional cost increase.
Value created when combined entities perform better than separately.
Expected deals/projects not yet closed.
Outcome beneficial to both sides.
Method widely accepted as superior.
History of past performance.
Delivered complete and ready to operate.
Product made by one firm and sold under another’s brand.
Unit responsible for costs only / for revenue and costs.
Company controlled by another (usually >50% of votes).
Company related through common ownership or control.
Company that controls subsidiaries.
Business jointly owned and controlled by two or more parties.
Official registration of a business with the authorities.
Permission to conduct specified activities (common in GCC).
Yearly shareholder meeting to approve accounts, appoint auditors, elect directors.
Meeting for major decisions (capital changes, amendments to articles).
Formal decision of the board.
Legal authorisation for someone to act on another’s behalf.
Person authorised to sign for the company.
Rules for who can approve what, up to which amounts.
Natural person who ultimately owns or controls an entity.
Person/entity with close links to the company (directors, owners, their companies).
Officer responsible for statutory compliance and board administration.
Director who is / is not also a manager.
Non-executive director without material ties to the company.
Authorisation to vote on someone’s behalf.
Shares traded / not traded on a stock exchange.
Entity registered in a special economic zone with specific rules (e.g., in the UAE).
Extension of a company in another location, not a separate legal entity.
Office allowed to promote but usually not to trade.
Separating a business unit into an independent company.
Group operating in unrelated industries.
Record of a transaction with debits and credits.
Master record of all accounts.
List of all ledger balances; debits must equal credits.
Structured list of all accounts used.
Expense incurred but not yet invoiced/paid.
Expense paid before the period it relates to.
Revenue earned, not yet invoiced.
Possible obligation depending on uncertain future events; disclosed, not recognised.
Cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment.
Expected value at the end of useful life.

terms.ar: الوارد أولاً صادر أولاً / المتوسط المرجح
terms.def: Inventory cost formulas (LIFO is not permitted under IFRS).
Estimated selling price less costs to complete and sell; inventory is held at lower of cost and NRV.
Receivables not expected to be collected.
Removing an asset (e.g., a receivable) from the books.
Comparing two records (e.g., bank statement vs ledger) and explaining differences.
Process of finalising the month’s accounts.
Size or nature of an item that could influence users’ decisions.
Combining parent and subsidiaries’ accounts as one economic entity.
Equity in a subsidiary not owned by the parent.
Tax effect of timing differences between accounting and tax rules.
Obligations not recognised as liabilities (guarantees, some commitments).
Correcting previously issued financial statements.

terms.ar: المعايير الدولية لإعداد التقارير المالية / معايير المحاسبة الدولية
terms.def: Standards issued by the IASB (IAS = older standards still in force).

terms.ar: المبادئ المحاسبية المقبولة عموماً في الولايات المتحدة
terms.def: US standards issued by FASB (codified in the ASC).
Today’s value of a future amount.
Value at a future date after compounding.
Rate used to convert future cash flows to present value.
Return shareholders require.
Interest rate on borrowings (after tax in WACC).
Ke = risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium.
Sensitivity of a stock’s returns to the market.
Return on a default-free government security.
Extra return investors require for holding equities.
Tax saved because interest is deductible.
Reduction in ownership % when new shares are issued.
Contractual interest on a bond.
Amount repaid at maturity.
Sensitivity of a bond’s price to interest-rate changes.
Difference between two rates or prices.
Collection of investments.
Index against which performance is measured.
Return above that explained by market risk.
Excess return per unit of volatility.

terms.ar: مركز شراء / مركز بيع على المكشوف
terms.def: Owning an asset / profiting from its fall.
Rising / falling market.
Profiting from price differences for the same asset.
Taking risk to profit from expected price moves.
Total value returned ÷ capital invested.
Assets managed by a fund manager.
Net asset value of a fund (per unit/share).
Bank officer responsible for a client relationship.
Body that approves credit decisions.
Written analysis recommending a credit decision.
Using a facility (taking the loan).
Amount currently drawn.
Unused capacity under a limit or covenant.
Fee on undrawn committed amounts.
Upfront fee for structuring a loan.
Period before repayments begin.
Repayment at maturity / large final instalment.
Event allowing lenders to accelerate the loan.
Demanding immediate repayment after default.
Lender’s agreement to overlook a breach.
Promise not to grant security to other lenders.
Ranking equally with other creditors.
Debt ranking behind senior debt.
Cash available for debt service ÷ debt service.
Loan amount ÷ collateral value.

terms.ar: حساب لنا لديكم / حساب لكم لدينا
terms.def: Bank’s account at another bank / another bank’s account with it.

terms.ar: رقم الحساب المصرفي الدولي / رمز البنك
terms.def: Account and bank identifiers for international payments.
Date funds become available / interest starts.
Latest time to submit payments for same-day processing.
Selling receivables to a factor for early cash.
Advancing funds against a bill of exchange before maturity.
International bank capital and liquidity framework (BCBS).
Bank capital ÷ risk-weighted assets.
Politically exposed person — higher AML risk.
Anti-money laundering / countering financing of terrorism.
Checking names, vessels, goods and countries against sanctions lists.
Interaction determining market price and quantity.
Price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
Value of the best alternative forgone.
Output per unit of input (e.g., per worker-hour).
Cost of producing one more unit.
Price indices for consumers / producers.
Falling general price level.
High inflation with stagnant growth.
Central bank’s main interest rate.
Central bank asset purchases to ease conditions.
Yields across maturities; inversion often precedes slowdowns.
Government spending above revenue.
Debt issued by a national government.
Fixed exchange rate to an anchor currency.
Official reduction in a pegged currency’s value.
Restrictions on moving money across borders.
Tax on imports (sometimes exports).
Quotas, licences, standards limiting trade.
Restrictions on dealings with countries, entities or persons.
Risk from political, economic or legal conditions in a country.
Risk that a government defaults or blocks payments.
Share of the labour force without work and seeking it.
Expansion, peak, contraction, trough.
Survey indicator; above 50 = expansion.
Qualified potential buyer.
Open opportunities, with values and stages.
Share moving from one stage to the next.
Selling a higher version / related products to the same customer.
How a brand is perceived relative to competitors.
Value from customer perception of a brand.
Plan for reaching and selling to target customers.
Description of the best-fit customer organisation.

terms.ar: طلب عرض / طلب تسعير / طلب معلومات
terms.def: Buyer’s requests for proposals / quotes / information.
Formal competitive bidding process.
Deals won ÷ deals decided.
Time from first contact to closing.
Sales target for a salesperson.
Payment based on sales achieved.
Setting a first number that influences the negotiation.
Something given up in negotiation.
Point beyond which you will not agree.
Exchanging one variable for another (price for volume).
Agreement to deal only with one party in a scope.
Preliminary document of intended terms.
Price reduction for quantity / refund after reaching volume.
Promise to give a customer terms at least as good as others.
Loyalty measure: % promoters − % detractors.
Network from raw materials to the end customer.
Process of sourcing and buying goods and services.
Buyer’s formal order document.
List of components for a product.
Order quantity minimising ordering + holding costs.
Unique stock item code.
Software for warehouse / transport management.
Transferring goods from inbound to outbound with minimal storage.
Full container load / less than container load.
Twenty- / forty-foot equivalent unit.
Non-negotiable air transport document.
Document certifying where goods were produced.
Details of packages, weights and contents.
